1:1.t: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the Persian name Khshayarsha, which the Greeks wrote as Xerxes. He is usually identified with Xerxes I, who reigned 486-465 BC. The KJV form is kept. Cush: the KJV's "Ethiopia", its usual rendering of the Hebrew Cush, a land south of Egypt; see Genesis 2:13.

The name of God: Esther is one of only two books of the Bible (with Song of Solomon) that never name God. There is no prayer, no mention of the law, the temple, or the covenant, though the Jews fast (4:16). Readers have long seen God at work in the book all the same, hidden behind "chance" events: a sleepless night (6:1), a well-timed lot (3:7), an orphan made queen. We translate what the text says and add nothing. The Greek Old Testament adds six long passages (in the Apocrypha as "Additions to Esther") that name God and include prayers; the KJV, following the Hebrew, does not include them in Esther.

1:2.t: and following "The citadel of Susa": the KJV's "Shushan the palace". Susa was one of the capitals of the Persian kings; the citadel was the fortified royal quarter, set apart from the city of Susa (3:15).

1:3.t: "The commanders of the armies": the KJV's "the power of Persia and Media". The third year of Xerxes was 483 BC.

1:4.t: "180 days": the display lasted half a year, perhaps while the king planned his war against Greece.

1:6.t: "Couches": the KJV's "beds", the couches guests reclined on at a banquet. The Hebrew names of the colors and stones are rare, and their exact meaning is uncertain.

1:7.t: "The king's generosity": the KJV's "the state of the king", literally "the hand of the king".

2:18.t: "The king's generosity": the KJV's "the state of the king", literally "the hand of the king".
"A holiday": the KJV's "a release". The Hebrew may mean a rest from work or a cancelling of taxes.

1:10.t: and following "Eunuchs": the KJV's "chamberlains". The Hebrew saris usually means a eunuch, a castrated man trusted to serve in the royal household, especially among the women. It can also mean simply a court official.

1:13.t: "Who understood the times": wise men who knew the customs and precedents, or perhaps astrologers who read the times.

1:14.t: "Who had personal access to the king": the KJV's "which saw the king's face".

1:19.t: "So that it cannot be changed": a law of the Medes and Persians could not be revoked (compare Daniel 6:8). That is why in chapter 8 the king cannot cancel Haman's decree, but can only issue a second decree that lets the Jews defend themselves.

8:8.t: "So that it cannot be changed": a law of the Medes and Persians could not be revoked (compare Daniel 6:8). That is why in chapter 8 the king cannot cancel Haman's decree, but can only issue a second decree that lets the Jews defend themselves.

1:22.t: "That this should be proclaimed in the language of every people": as in the KJV. The Hebrew can also mean that each man should speak his own language in his home, and many modern Bibles read it that way.

2:3.t: "Harem": the KJV's "the house of the women". Hegai: the KJV spells it Hege here and Hegai in 2:8 and 2:15. "Beauty treatments": the KJV's "things for purification", cosmetics and ointments.

2:5.t: "Benjaminite": the KJV's "Benjamite". Mordecai's line goes back to Kish, the father of King Saul (1 Samuel 9:1).

2:6.t: "He had been carried away": the Hebrew can refer to Mordecai or to his great-grandfather Kish. The exile with Jeconiah was in 597 BC, more than a century before Xerxes, so it most likely means Mordecai's family.

2:7.t: Hadassah is Hebrew for "myrtle". Esther may come from the Persian word for "star", or from the name of the goddess Ishtar.

"Took her as his own daughter" (Hebrew laqach lebat): the same verb, laqach, "take", is used for Esther being "taken" to the palace (2:8, 2:16). The book uses it without saying whether Esther consented, and readers differ on how much choice she had.

2:9.t: "Her portions of food": the KJV's "such things as belonged to her".

2:16.t: Tebeth is the tenth month, December to January. The seventh year of Xerxes was 479 BC, four years after Vashti was removed.

2:19.t: "Sitting at the king's gate": a sign that Mordecai held an office at the palace; the gate was where officials did business.

2:21.t: Bigthan is spelled Bigthana in 6:2 in the Hebrew and the KJV.

6:2.t: Bigthan is spelled Bigthana in 6:2 in the Hebrew and the KJV.

2:23.t: and following "Gallows": as in the KJV. The Hebrew ets means "tree" or "pole" (the KJV says "hanged on a tree" in 2:23). Persian executions often meant impaling or hanging the body on a tall stake. "Gallows" is kept throughout for clarity.

5:14.t: and following "Gallows": as in the KJV. The Hebrew ets means "tree" or "pole" (the KJV says "hanged on a tree" in 2:23). Persian executions often meant impaling or hanging the body on a tall stake. "Gallows" is kept throughout for clarity.

3:1.t: "Agagite": a descendant of Agag, the king of the Amalekites whom Saul spared (1 Samuel 15). Mordecai, of Saul's family, and Haman, of Agag's, take up an old conflict (Exodus 17:14-16).

3:2.t: "Bowed down and paid honor": the reason Mordecai refused is not given. Bowing to a superior was normal in Israel too (Genesis 23:7), so it may have been because Haman was an Amalekite, or because Persian custom gave such honor a religious meaning.

3:7.t: Nisan is the first month, March to April. The twelfth year of Xerxes was 474 BC. Adar is the twelfth month, February to March. The lot fell almost a year away, giving time for what follows.

"Pur" and "Purim": pur is not a Hebrew word but a Babylonian one (puru, "lot"), which the writer explains for Hebrew readers: "pur, that is, the lot" (Hebrew goral). Casting lots was a way of choosing a lucky day. Haman trusted the lot to pick the day of the Jews' ruin; the feast that remembers their rescue is named, with some irony, after his lot. Proverbs 16:33 gives the Hebrew view: "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD."

3:9.t: KJV: "ten thousand talents of silver", a huge sum, perhaps two-thirds of the empire's yearly revenue.

3:10.t: "Signet ring": the KJV's "ring", used to seal documents with the king's authority.

3:12.t: "Satraps": the KJV's "lieutenants", the governors of the great regions of the empire.

8:9.t: "Satraps": the KJV's "lieutenants", the governors of the great regions of the empire.
Sivan is the third month, May to June, about two months after Haman's decree.

9:3.t: "Satraps": the KJV's "lieutenants", the governors of the great regions of the empire.

3:13.t: "Couriers": the KJV's "posts", the royal mounted messengers of the Persian road system.

8:10.t: "Couriers": the KJV's "posts", the royal mounted messengers of the Persian road system.
"Young dromedaries": the Hebrew words are rare and are thought to mean royal horses or swift mounts bred for the king's service.

8:14.t: "Couriers": the KJV's "posts", the royal mounted messengers of the Persian road system.

3:15.t: "Was thrown into confusion": the KJV's "was perplexed".

4:1.t: Tearing one's clothes and wearing sackcloth and ashes were signs of grief and mourning.

4:5.t: Hathach: the KJV spells it Hatach.

4:6.t: Hathach: the KJV spells it Hatach.

4:9.t: Hathach: the KJV spells it Hatach.

4:10.t: Hathach: the KJV spells it Hatach.

4:11.t: "The gold scepter": the KJV's "golden sceptre". Even the queen could be put to death for coming to the king uninvited.

4:16.t: "Three days, night or day": counted in the Jewish way, part of a day as a day, which is why Esther goes to the king "on the third day" (5:1).

"If I perish, I perish" (Hebrew kaasher avadti avadti): the verb avad, "perish", is the same word used in Haman's decree "to destroy, kill, and wipe out" (3:13, "wipe out" there translating the causative form). Esther accepts for herself the fate decreed for her people.

5:1.t: "The king's hall": the KJV's "the king's house", the throne room.

5:6.t: "As they were drinking wine": the KJV's "at the banquet of wine", the drinking that followed the meal.

7:2.t: "As they were drinking wine": the KJV's "at the banquet of wine", the drinking that followed the meal.

7:9.t: Harbonah: the KJV spells him Harbona in 1:10 and Harbonah here.

6:1.t: "The king could not sleep": the Hebrew says "the king's sleep fled". The story turns on this sleepless night.

6:8.t: "The royal crown that is set on his head": as in the KJV, the king's crown. The Hebrew can also mean that a royal crest was set on the horse's head, as Persian reliefs show, and many modern Bibles read it that way.

6:12.t: "With his head covered": a sign of shame and grief (2 Samuel 15:30).

7:4.t: "Although the enemy could never make up for the king's loss": as in the KJV. The Hebrew can also mean "for our trouble would not be worth bothering the king with", and many modern Bibles read it that way.

7:8.t: "Reclining": guests reclined on couches at a meal. "They covered Haman's face": a sign that he was condemned.

8:11.t: "Along with their little ones and women": as in the KJV, these words echo Haman's decree (3:13) word for word. Some read them as the attackers' families, others as the Jews' own families whom the attackers threatened; the Hebrew allows both. Chapter 9 records only men killed.

8:17.t: "Became Jews": the Hebrew word occurs only here. It may mean converted to the Jewish faith or claimed to be Jews.

9:7.t: Vaizatha: the KJV spells it Vajezatha. In Hebrew Bibles these ten names are written in a column, one under another.

9:10.t: "They did not lay their hands on the plunder": though the king's decree allowed it (8:11). This contrasts with Saul, who took plunder from the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:9).

9:15.t: "They did not lay their hands on the plunder": though the king's decree allowed it (8:11). This contrasts with Saul, who took plunder from the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:9).

9:16.t: "They did not lay their hands on the plunder": though the king's decree allowed it (8:11). This contrasts with Saul, who took plunder from the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:9).

9:19.t: "A holiday": the KJV's "a good day". "Gifts of food": the KJV's "portions".
Jews in villages kept Purim on the 14th of Adar; those in walled cities like Susa on the 15th. Jewish custom still keeps this difference.

9:22.t: "A holiday": the KJV's "a good day". "Gifts of food": the KJV's "portions".

9:26.t: Purim is the Hebrew plural of pur, "lot": "the Lots".

9:29.t: "This second letter": the first was Mordecai's letter in verse 20.

9:31.t: "Their fasts and their lamenting": the KJV's "the fastings and their cry". Jewish custom keeps the Fast of Esther on the 13th of Adar, the day before Purim.

"Remembered" (Hebrew zakar): to remember in Hebrew is more than to recall; it means to act on behalf of someone, to keep a person or event in mind (see Nehemiah 5:19). The feast keeps the deliverance alive in each generation by acting it out again, not just recalling it.

10:3.t: "Second only to": the KJV's "next unto". "Well loved by": the KJV's "accepted of". "The good of his people": the KJV's "the wealth of his people", in the old sense of well-being.

9:24.t: "Pur" and "Purim": pur is not a Hebrew word but a Babylonian one (puru, "lot"), which the writer explains for Hebrew readers: "pur, that is, the lot" (Hebrew goral). Casting lots was a way of choosing a lucky day. Haman trusted the lot to pick the day of the Jews' ruin; the feast that remembers their rescue is named, with some irony, after his lot. Proverbs 16:33 gives the Hebrew view: "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD."

4:14.t: "From another place" (Hebrew mimmaqom acher): some readers take "place" (maqom) as a hidden reference to God, since later Jewish writings use HaMaqom, "the Place", as a name for God. Others take it simply to mean "from some other source". The words do not settle it, and we leave them plain. "Relief" (revach) means room to breathe, a widening after being hemmed in.

"For such a time as this" (Hebrew laet kazot): Mordecai does not say God put Esther in the palace, but asks "who knows?" The words hold out the possibility of purpose without claiming certainty. The verse is often quoted to mean that each person is placed for a purpose; in its setting it is a call to one woman to risk her life for her people at one moment.

6:13.t: "You will surely fall" (Hebrew naphol tippol): a doubled verb for emphasis, "falling you will fall". Haman's wise men see that the Jews are not an ordinary people to be fought, though again God is not named.

9:1.t: "The reverse happened" (Hebrew venahafokh hu, "and it was turned around"): the key idea of the book. Everything Haman planned is overturned: the honor he wanted goes to Mordecai, the gallows he built is used for him, the day set for the Jews' destruction becomes their deliverance. The same verb, haphak, "turn", is used in 9:22 of sorrow "turned" into joy.

9:28.t: "Remembered" (Hebrew zakar): to remember in Hebrew is more than to recall; it means to act on behalf of someone, to keep a person or event in mind (see Nehemiah 5:19). The feast keeps the deliverance alive in each generation by acting it out again, not just recalling it.
